reason: The text depicts Yahweh as a particular, personal, and concrete deity rather than universal, omniscient, or abstract. Yahweh identifies himself specifically as 'the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'—tied to a particular lineage and people. The narrative shows God responding to the specific cry of the Israelites, focused on their particular affliction in Egypt rather than universal concerns. Furthermore, Yahweh manifests physically in the burning bush and speaks directly to Moses in an intimate, personal encounter (Moses hides his face because he fears looking at God), indicating a concrete rather than abstract presence. While the text suggests God perceives events ('I have seen the affliction...I have heard the cry'), this is depicted through active observation rather than the kind of comprehensive omniscience characteristic of abstract universal deities.
